note: Adds a hedge ("Perhaps") to an unhedged conditional and drops "if necessary" from the foregone benefits.
replacement: To have a right, then, is, I hold, to have something that society ought to defend me in possessing. Suppose the objector goes on to ask why society ought to do so. I can give him no reason but general utility. Suppose that expression does not seem to convey enough of the strength of the obligation, or to explain the peculiar energy of the feeling. If so, the cause is that the sentiment is composed of an animal element, the thirst for retaliation, as well as a rational one. That thirst draws its intensity, and its moral justification, from the extraordinarily important and impressive kind of utility at stake. The interest concerned is security, which everyone feels to be the most vital of all interests. Almost every other earthly benefit is needed by one person and not by another, and many can, if necessary, be cheerfully done without, or replaced by something else. Security, however, no human being can possibly do without. All our immunity from evil depends on it, as does the whole value of every good beyond the passing moment. For if whoever was momentarily stronger than we are could take everything from us the next instant, nothing but the gratification of the instant would be worth anything to us. Now this most indispensable of all necessaries, after physical nutriment, cannot be had unless the machinery that provides it is kept constantly at work. So we claim that our fellow creatures must join in making the very groundwork of our existence safe for us. Feelings gather around this claim that are far more intense than those in any of the more common cases of utility, and so the difference in degree (as often happens in psychology) becomes a real difference in kind. The claim acquires that character of absoluteness, that apparent infinity, that incommensurability with every other consideration, which marks the difference between the feeling of right and wrong and the feeling of ordinary expediency and inexpediency. These feelings are so powerful, and we count so positively on a responsive feeling in others (since all are alike interested), that _ought_ and _should_ grow into _must_. Recognized indispensability becomes a moral necessity, like a physical one, and often equal to it in binding force.
